newsitem.title: USA: HTA fallout has changed U.S. ag dealings - trade.
newsitem.headline: HTA fallout has changed U.S. ag dealings - trade.

text.p: Losses that stemmed from the use of hedge-to-arrive (HTA) contracts in 1996 have permanently changed the way country elevators and producers do business, agriculture consultants told an annual grain trade conference Monday.

"I think the days of the friendly handshake or the deal over the telephone are long gone in this industry," said John Sen Chu, director of financial risk strategy for New York-based KPMG Peat Marwick LLP.
Sen Chu's comments came during the National Grain and Feed Association's (NGFA) annual country elevator council meeting.
As a result of the HTA controversy, country elevator operators and producers will have to take added precautions when entering into cash grain transactions, bankers and consultants told the meeting.
"The whole commodity industry... is behind in terms of risk management," Sen Chu said.

To avoid the potential heavy losses associated with this year's volatile grain markets and cash hybrid contracts, elevators must know their customers, put everything in writing and have an attorney review all contracts, said David Barrett, counsel for public affairs with the NGFA.
"You're not of sound mind if you're not putting things in writing," Barrett said.
NGFA offers arbitration for members to help settle future disputes, but Barrett said an NGFA arbitration clause must be included in the contract.

In an attempt to ease concern over HTAs, elevators seeking operating capital from banks should divulge the extent of hedge-to-arrive exposure, said Brian Wise, vice president, sales manager for Key Bank in Indianapolis.
Elevators should also use banks to perform credit inquiries on their farmer customers and should also suggest that farmers do the same on elevators.
Wise said that because of the ongoing HTA controversy, grain companies will receive more scrutiny in the next six months than they ever have.
